findings.title: The docs/08 explorer's assumed costs are 2-21x below the measured Linux per-process cost and about 8x below the measured store cost, so its Status column is not evidence of being in budget
findings.evidence: docs/08:21 'Cost of one bulk sample, assumed: 1.5 ms plus 0.012 ms for each process'; :22 '+0.2 points for the store and the API'; :9 'assumed costs, not from measurements. Phase 0 replaces the assumptions'; :46 '1 s | 10 s | 300 | 0.7% ... | In budget'. Re-ran uv run python docs/review/probes/b-measurement/model_tables.py (arithmetic only), identical to saved: 'direct /proc, stat + statm + io 0.0517 ms = 4.3 times'; 'psutil provider, snapshot() 0.2488 ms = 20.7 times'; 'store adds about 15.9 ms per tick = 1.6 points at 1 s (assumed: 0.2 points for the store and the API)'; 'whole tick + raw store 36.0 ms ... 1s 3.60% (over)'; '10% of 300 processes hot: ... 1s 0.68%'; 'whole tick + raw store, psutil fallback 95.1 ms ... 5s 1.90% (over)'. measure/collector_footprint.out.txt: '14.1% of one core' (psutil provider, 447 processes), '120 bytes per sample row overall (brief assumes 90)'.
findings.impact: The explorer is the only cost table the owner sees, and it understates every part. On Linux the budget at a 1 s active interval holds only if the hot set really limits per-tick reads: 3.60% when every process is handled every tick, 0.68% with a 10% hot set. The psutil fallback, measured here on Linux, is over the 1% idle limit at 5 s; Windows is unmeasured. This is not a gate failure yet: P1 replaces the psutil provider, and docs/17:230 already asks P0 to say whether the numbers are unrealistic.
findings.proposed_change: docs/08 'Sample time explorer': after the assumptions paragraph, add the measured Linux costs labelled 'Linux, baseline code, one 8-core laptop; Windows unmeasured until P0': per process 0.025 ms (stat only), 0.052 ms (stat+statm+io), 0.25 ms (psutil); Python work after the snapshot about 0.033 ms per process; raw store about 10 ms per tick at 300 processes; 120 bytes per row. State that the Status column comes from the assumed costs and is not a budget check. docs/15 P0 and docs/17:268: measure the whole tick (snapshot, deltas, attribution, store) for each provider, including the psutil fallback.
findings.cost: About 10 lines in docs/08, one sentence in docs/15 and docs/17.
findings.verification: Re-ran model_tables.py: output identical. Re-read docs/08:7-54, docs/17:40,71,230. Refutation: docs/08:9 and :11 already label the explorer a model with assumed costs that P0 replaces, and docs/17:230 asks P0 to report unrealistic numbers, so the design anticipates the gap. docs/17:71 says that on Linux the hot set is read at the active interval and the cold set at the cold interval. With a 10% hot set the measured whole tick plus store is 0.68% at 1 s, so the headline claim that the 'In budget' row is over budget holds only when every process is read every tick. The 14.1% figure comes from the baseline psutil provider, which P1 replaces (docs/17:40 'psutil is the fallback and the cross-check, not the hot path'), so it is not a P1 gate failure. The 15.9 ms store cost is the difference between two separate runs and is approximate. Severity downgraded from high to medium.

findings.title: The Rust switching rule does not say what 'one full sample' or 'holds 80 MB' measures, and its 10 ms is a third of the budget it stands in for, so it can point either way
findings.evidence: docs/11:21-22 'One full sample of 300 processes takes more than 10 ms in phase 0.' / 'The collector process holds more than 80 MB.' (the lead cites :69-70); docs/17:56 'measure one full sample. If it takes more than 10 ms at 300 processes, or the collector holds more than 80 MB, stop and tell me'; docs/11:7 'its cost is the system call, not the interpreter' (the lead cites :55). model_tables.out.txt section 4 (rerun identical): 'direct /proc, stat only 7.5 ms -> stay'; 'direct /proc, stat + statm + io 15.5 ms -> switch'; 'psutil provider, snapshot() 74.6 ms -> switch'; 'collector memory, resident 39 MB -> stay'; '10 ms per sample is 1.0% of a core at 1 s and 0.2% at 5 s; the budget itself allows 30 ms per tick at 1 s (3%) and 50 ms per tick at 5 s (1%)'. Section 3: whole tick plus store 36.0 ms against a 15.5 ms snapshot, so 57% of the tick comes after the snapshot.
findings.impact: The result depends on choices the rule leaves open: the provider, the part of the tick (snapshot only, or with deltas, attribution and store), the memory figure and the machine. On this machine's numbers each choice changes the outcome. The rule can call for Rust while the budget holds (a 15.5 ms snapshot is 1.55% at 1 s). It can also say stay while the whole collector is over budget (a 7.5 ms snapshot inside a 36 ms tick). It is the owner's trigger ('stop and tell me'), so the owner still decides, but on a figure that may be the wrong one.
findings.proposed_change: docs/11 'When to switch the collector to Rust' and docs/17:56: replace the first two bullets with: 'In phase 0, run the collector (snapshot, deltas, attribution and raw-store writes) for 10 minutes with 300 processes on the owner's Windows machine, with the provider that will ship and with the psutil fallback. Report its process CPU time as a share of one core at the active and idle intervals, and its private bytes (Windows) or USS (Linux). Switch if the CPU share exceeds the budget (3% active, 1% idle) at the default cadence, or memory exceeds 80 MB.' Qualify docs/11:7: on Linux /proc is read per process, and Python work after the snapshot is about half the tick.
findings.cost: About 5 lines in docs/11 and docs/17.
findings.decision_question: Should the Rust trigger be the budget itself, or should the 10 ms snapshot rule stay? The budget version compares the whole collector's CPU share with 3% and 1%, and a named memory figure with 80 MB, on the owner's Windows PC. Keeping the 10 ms rule would mean defining what 'one full sample' includes. Recommendation: use the budget. The 10 ms rule stands in for it, and the measured numbers show the two disagree in both directions.
findings.verification: Re-read docs/11. The bullets are at lines 21-22, not 69-70, and the 'system call' sentence is at line 7, not 55. Re-read docs/17:56 and :230. Re-ran model_tables.py: output identical. Searched docs/ for a definition of 'full sample': the only other mention is docs/17:230 'Measure the cost of one full sample in phase 0'. Refutation: the rule is the owner's own trigger to be told, not an automatic switch, so no gate is broken. Severity downgraded from high to medium. The memory branch never decides on Linux, where the collector measured 39 MB resident.

findings.title: The leak acceptance ('50 MB an hour flagged within 2 hours') sits exactly on the default threshold of 50 MiB/h, its units are undefined, and the earliest possible flag comes after 2 hours
findings.evidence: docs/01:18 'A leak of 50 MB an hour is flagged within 2 hours'; docs/17:154 'growth of 50 MB an hour must be flagged within two hours'; core/config.py:121 'min_slope: Rate = 50 * 1024**2 / 3600.0'; core/units.py:56 'Units are binary'; analysis/growth.py:73 'duration < min_duration_s', :78 'slope < min_slope_per_s'; docs/17:123 'A bucket is final 30 seconds after it ends'. uv run python docs/review/probes/verify-5/leak_checks.py: '100 MiB/h, 120 buckets spanning 119 min: not enough data yet' / '121 buckets spanning 120 min: FLAGGED'; '50 MiB/h ... noise 0 MB: 100% noise 5 MB: 45% noise 30 MB: 45%'; '50 MB/h decimal ... 0% ... 0% ... 14%'; '55 MiB/h ... 100% 100% 97%'. Re-ran b-measurement/growth_acceptance.py and e-baseline/growth_cases.py: both identical to saved.
findings.impact: Job 3's acceptance and the P3 trigger fixture fail as written. A load generator leaking 50 MiB/h is flagged in about 45% of 2-hour windows once there is any noise. One leaking 50 decimal MB/h is never flagged without noise. Even a fast leak cannot be flagged until 2 h 01 min 30 s after it starts, when the 121st minute bucket becomes final.
findings.proposed_change: docs/01:18, the docs/15 P3 gate and docs/17:154: state the acceptance as a rate clearly above min_slope, with a reachable delay, for example 'a leak of 75 MiB an hour is flagged within 2 h 5 min'. The alternative is to lower Leak.min_slope (core/config.py:121, docs/08:88). Say in docs/12 or in docs/08 'How configuration behaves' that MB in settings and acceptance criteria means 1024 x 1024 bytes. Name the leak window precisely; docs/06:64 says only '2 to 48 h back'.
findings.cost: About three sentences of docs, or one default in config.py.
findings.decision_question: Raise the acceptance rate (for example 75 MiB/h within 2 h 5 min, with the 50 MiB/h threshold unchanged), or lower the threshold (for example 30 MiB/h, keeping 50 MiB/h in the acceptance)? Recommendation: raise the acceptance rate. A lower threshold also raises the plateau test's false flags (M4). The two leads disagree here: B recommends lowering the threshold, E recommends raising the rate.
findings.verification: Re-read config.py:119-121, units.py:29-35 and :56, growth.py:63-84, docs/01:18 and docs/17:123,154. Wrote and ran verify-5/leak_checks.py with 200 seeds per noisy cell; results as quoted. Re-ran growth_acceptance.py and growth_cases.py: both identical. Searched the glossary and docs/08 for a definition of MB: none. Refutation: if 'within 2 hours' were measured from the first observable bucket, the timing complaint would shrink to 1.5 minutes. The threshold equality and the units problem stand on their own, so severity stays high. docs/06:64 does state a loose leak window ('2 to 48 h back'), so the claim that the window is unstated is softened to 'imprecise'.

findings.title: The plateau test clears or flags by noise: the brief's own browser warm-up is falsely flagged at its stated noise, and a leak that grows in 2-hour steps is never flagged with a 2-hour window
findings.evidence: analysis/growth.py:45-53 'cut = int(len(xs) * (1 - tail))' ... 'theil_sen(xs[cut:], ys[cut:]) < ratio * overall', with tail 1/3 and ratio 0.25 (the lead cites :157-165, which do not exist in this 110-line file). docs/07:24 'Browser: 3.6 GB plus 0.9 x (1 - e^(-t / 0.35 h)) GB, with noise of up to 0.04 GB either way'; docs/01:18 'and a cache warming up is not'. verify-5/leak_checks.out.txt (sliding 2 h window, a check every 5 min over hours 2-4, 60 seeds): 'noise-free warm-up (a fixture a builder might write): flagged=False'; 'minute buckets noise +/- 5 MB: 0 of 60', '+/-20 MB: 11 of 60', '+/-40 MB: 34 of 60 runs falsely flagged'; '5-minute points as in docs/07 noise +/-40 MB: 51 of 60'; 'staircase +256 MiB every 120 min ... sliding 2 h window: flagged in 0 of 121 checks', 'growing window: flagged in 53 of 121 checks'. growth_acceptance.py rerun identical (section 9: 'noise 40 MB: sliding 34 of 60 runs').
findings.impact: Job 3's rule that a warm-up is not flagged fails in about half of runs when the noise on each bucket is the brief's own +/-40 MB. The P3 quiet fixture passes if the builder writes the warm-up without noise, so the gate hides the problem. A leak that grows in steps reads as 'levelled off' under a 2-hour window.
findings.proposed_change: Plan a P3 task: replace the ratio test in growth.py plateaued(). The new test should not compare a noisy 40-point tail with a fraction of the whole-window slope; for example, require the tail slope's lower confidence bound to clear min_slope, or require a minimum tail span. Make the detector window span at least two steps of a staircase. docs/17:161 and the docs/15 P3 gate: list as fixtures, all on the minute tier, the docs/07 warm-up with +/-40 MB noise per bucket (quiet) and a staircase leak (trigger).
findings.cost: A few lines of fixture wording in docs now; the detector change and tuning as one planned task.
findings.verification: Re-read growth.py:45-84. Wrote leak_checks.py to test the noise assumption. At +/-5 MB per bucket the warm-up is never falsely flagged (0 of 60 runs), so the result depends on how much noise survives into a bucket; per-second noise averaged into minute means would be smaller. docs/07:24 states +/-40 MB on 5-minute points, and at that resolution 51 of 60 runs are falsely flagged, so the brief's own example fails as the brief draws it. The staircase miss depends on the window: a growing window flags it in 53 of 121 checks, and docs/06:64 ('2 to 48 h back') leaves the window open. The garbage-collection sawtooth case is left out because the lead itself calls it arguable. Severity kept at high.

findings.title: The slow-growth check has no threshold of its own; with the only slope setting (leak.min_slope) it cannot flag any leak that the hourly check would miss
findings.evidence: core/config.py:124-125 'class SlowGrowth(Record): window: Duration = 7 * 86400.0', with no slope field; docs/08:88-89 list only leak.min_slope 50MB/h and slow_growth.window 7d; docs/17:155 'fit the daily minimum of memory over at least 7 days. This catches leaks too slow for the check above'; docs/16:269 (R34 fix). verify-5/leak_checks.out.txt: "SlowGrowth fields: ['window']"; '8 d of hourly buckets from 00:00: 8 daily minimums spanning 7 d; with leak.min_slope: growth is below the threshold; with 5 MiB/h: FLAGGED'; '7 d of hourly buckets from 00:00: 7 daily minimums spanning 6 d; with leak.min_slope: not enough data yet'. b-measurement/baseline_table.py rerun identical.
findings.impact: With the defaults, the P3 gate fixture 'a leak too slow for the hourly check' fails, so R34's fix does not work as configured. A builder has to invent a threshold that no document gives.
findings.proposed_change: core/config.py SlowGrowth: add min_slope (for example 5 MiB/h, below Leak.min_slope), and define the window as a count of daily minimums (at least 7 minima, which needs 8 days of hourly buckets) rather than a 7-day span. docs/08:89: add the min_slope row. docs/17:155 and :180: state both values. Add a test with a 10 MiB/h leak over 8 days.
findings.cost: About 6 lines in config.py, two rows in docs/08, one test.
findings.verification: Re-read config.py:119-137, docs/08:87-90, docs/17:155,180 and docs/14:352. Grepped docs/ for any slow-growth threshold: none. Ran leak_checks.py (section M5). Refutation: the 'span of 6 days' problem arises only if the builder passes the 7-day window as min_duration; a builder who treats 7 minima as enough avoids it, so that part is conditional. The missing threshold is not conditional. leak.min_slope is the only slope setting, and any leak it flags over 7 days the hourly check flags too, so with it the slow check adds nothing. Severity kept at high; verdict changed to 'confirmed with changes' because the span sub-claim depends on wiring.

findings.title: The usual range has no default floor and an ambiguous one: an idle series gets a zero-width range, docs/07 and usual_range() put the floor on different quantities, and the statistic baselined is never named
findings.evidence: docs/07:36 'The deviation is never taken as less than 0.03 GB', a floor on the MAD (the lead cites :116). analysis/growth.py:98 'spread = max(floor, _MAD_TO_SIGMA * median(...))', a floor on the scaled spread; :91 'floor: float = 0.0'. config.py:128-131: Baseline has no floor. verify-5/config_and_baseline.out.txt: "Baseline settings: ['learning_period', 'sensitivity', 'window']"; 'idle workload, 20 minutes at 0.000 cores and one at 0.001: (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)'; 'day 8, docs/07 sentence (floor on the deviation): 3.242 to 3.598; usual_range(floor=0.03): 3.300 to 3.540; docs/07 table prints 3.25 to 3.60'. baseline_table.py rerun identical: 'floor on the scaled spread ... days flagged: [14, 23, ...]'; on minute buckets, lognormal cores: '61 of 1440 ordinary minutes fall outside'. docs/17:156 'computed from minute buckets' against docs/07:31 'daily peak memory'.
findings.impact: R11's near-zero-spread problem returns for any idle workload: with CPU at 0, every non-zero minute is an anomaly. The two readings of the floor give half-widths of 0.178 GB and 0.120 GB, so docs/07's day 14 is inside the range under one reading and outside under the other. If single minute buckets of a skewed CPU series were compared with the range, about 4% of minutes would be flagged (this assumes a lognormal shape).
findings.proposed_change: docs/07:36 and the usual_range docstring: say which quantity the floor bounds (the scaled spread or the MAD), and give a floor per metric. core/config.py Baseline: add per-metric floors with non-zero defaults (for example 0.05 cores and 32 MiB), plus rows in docs/08. docs/17:156: name the value compared with the range (for example hourly p95 or daily peak, built from minute buckets), and require an anomaly to persist, for example for 3 consecutive values. Regenerate the docs/07 table from usual_range(), or mark it approximate.
findings.cost: About 10 lines across docs/07, docs/08, docs/17 and config.py.
findings.verification: Re-read growth.py:87-99, config.py:128-131, docs/07:29-74 and docs/17:156. Recomputed day 8 in config_and_baseline.py. The sentence's reading gives 3.242 to 3.598 against the table's 3.25 to 3.60, close given the rounded inputs. The code's reading gives 3.300 to 3.540, which is not close. Refutation: docs/07:5 calls the data illustrative, so the table mismatch on its own would be low. The 4% minute false-alarm figure rests on an assumed lognormal shape and on comparing single minutes, which no document specifies. The zero-width range for an idle series is shown directly. Severity kept at medium; the lead's line numbers (07:116, growth.py:203/210) are corrected here.

findings.title: The baseline's raw reader and its rollup put boundary samples in different buckets, so building a bucket from that bucket's read loses one sample and fails the 0.1% hourly gate at the default 5 s idle cadence
findings.evidence: store/raw.py:199 'WHERE ts > ? AND ts <= ?' (by end time); store/rollup.py:110 'bucket_start(sample.taken_at - sample.interval_s / 2, width_s)' (by the middle of the interval). Neither docs/06 nor docs/17 states a convention. docs/17:269 'CPU-hours from the hourly tier match the raw sum within 0.1%'. uv run python docs/review/probes/verify-5/rollup_and_histogram.py (steady 1 core, first tick 0.3 of an interval past the boundary): '3600 5 s 0.3x 2 3595 3600 3600 -0.139%'; '3600 10 s 0.3x ... -0.278%'; '60 1 s 0.3x 2 59 60 60 -1.667%'; '60 5 s 0.3x ... -8.333%'; at 0.7x '+0.000%' with 1 bucket back. b-measurement/rollup_conventions.py rerun identical ('idle 5 s ... worst 0.788%' for a bursty load).
findings.impact: A server that reads each minute or hour with RawFile.workload_samples and rolls it up, using the two baseline functions the builder is told to extend, drops one sample per bucket. This happens whenever ticks fall in the first half of an interval after the boundary. The rollup also returns a one-sample fragment of the previous bucket; if that is written, it replaces the real previous bucket, since 'recomputing a bucket gives the same row'. The minute tier then misses 1.7% of CPU at 1 s and 8.3% at 5 s, and the P1 hourly gate fails at the 5 s idle cadence even for a steady load (-0.139%). The collector's tick fixes the phase, so the loss is systematic, not random.
findings.proposed_change: Use one convention in both functions. For example, store/raw.py workload_samples selects 'ts - interval_s/2 >= start AND ts - interval_s/2 < end', which is the rollup's middle-of-interval rule. Add a test that reads one hour, rolls it up, and gets exactly one bucket equal to the whole-day rollup's bucket. docs/06 'What every bucket records': 'a sample belongs to the bucket that holds the middle of its interval'. docs/17:269: the raw sum is the sum of the samples assigned to that hour by the same rule. The lead's proposal to split samples across bucket edges is not needed and would introduce an estimate.
findings.cost: About 3 lines in raw.py, one test, and one sentence each in docs/06 and docs/17.
findings.verification: Re-read rollup.py:100-123 and raw.py:195-216. The lead's probe docstring names both rules, but its finding presents the gap as an unstated test convention. Wrote rollup_and_histogram.py (m7) to simulate a per-bucket read followed by roll_up for a steady load at two phases. Losses occur only when the phase is under half an interval, are exactly one interval per bucket, and come with a fragment bucket. Severity raised from medium to high because the shipped functions, combined in the obvious way, fail the P1 gate at the default 5 s idle cadence. Rejected the sub-claim that 'a 30-minute soak never completes an hour bucket': a soak that crosses an hour boundary does finalize a partly covered hour bucket, and the 0.1% check can also run as a unit test over a synthetic day.

findings.title: The P1 per-process 5% gate and the P2 2% gate use the product's own source as the reference, so neither can see CPU that escapes the group or that the collector never reads
findings.evidence: docs/17:269 'per-process figures agree with kernel counters (performance counters on Windows, /proc on Linux) within 5%'; docs/17:71 'On Linux, read /proc directly'; docs/17:62 'The kernel's totals for the group are authoritative'; docs/17:270 and docs/15:17 'charged within 2% of the kernel's total'. learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/procthread/job-objects (re-fetched): 'After a process is associated with a job, by default any child processes it creates using CreateProcess are also associated with the job. (Child processes created using Win32_Process.Create are not associated with the job.)'. a-linux/cgroup_scope.out.txt shows an independent reference that agrees: 'payload CPU seconds, kernel: 0.646515' against 'payload CPU seconds, wait4: 0.646941'. reconcile_terms.out.txt: 'one tick is 10 ms'; 'nanosecond run time per process (schedstat) present: True'.
findings.impact: P2's clause compares the group total with itself. A process outside the group, whether started before assignment or created through WMI on Windows, is missing from both sides, so the gate passes with a wrong tagged total (job 1). P1's Linux clause checks only parsing and delta arithmetic. Neither gate names a window or a minimum CPU level, and /proc times come in 10 ms ticks, so a per-tick comparison for a small process fails on rounding alone.
findings.proposed_change: docs/15 P1 and P2, and docs/17:269-270: use the load generator's own accounting as the reference. P1: each burner reports its own CPU seconds (getrusage RUSAGE_SELF on Linux, GetProcessTimes on Windows) at known instants. Over 10 minutes, Submeter's stored CPU for that process agrees within 5% or 0.05 s, whichever is larger, for processes above 10% of a core. P2: the generator reports its children's summed CPU (wait4 or RUSAGE_CHILDREN on Linux; GetProcessTimes on handles kept open on Windows). The run's stored CPU equals that sum plus the generator's own time within 2%, and a grandchild started in the command's first millisecond is a member of the group (IsProcessInJob, cgroup.procs). Keep the kernel and performance-counter comparison as a parsing check only.
findings.cost: About 10 lines in docs/15 and docs/17, plus a reporting requirement on the load generator.
findings.verification: Re-read docs/17:62,71,269-270, docs/15:13,17 and R10 at docs/16:109-113, which chose kernel counters but says nothing about independence. Re-fetched the Microsoft Job Objects page; both quoted sentences are present. Read a-linux/cgroup_scope.out.txt. Refutation: the P1 per-process comparison is more than a copy test. It can catch rows suppressed by the change threshold (docs/17:111), delta errors, and stale cold-set rows read at a different instant, so G's claim that it cannot catch stale cold-set rows is overstated. What it cannot catch is CPU of processes the collector never sees (R01); the reconciliation invariant covers that instead. P2's clause is self-referential as written. G#1's high was downgraded to medium: the gate is weak, but a wrong number also needs a separate escape defect, such as the launcher's assignment race, which another lens reports. Whether the Windows PDH counters share a source with the bulk snapshot is unverified. The hot_cpu_threshold sub-claim (0.5% of a core is half a tick per second) is real but affects only how often processes move in and out of the hot set, not a number.

findings.title: The verdict rules exist in two disagreeing tables, 'signals disagree' and 'maximum frequency' are undefined, and verdict.thresholds accepts any key
findings.evidence: docs/02:69 'The rules are checked in this order and the first match wins'. docs/02:73-77: Thermal 'Frequency below 80% of maximum' (no load condition); Memory 'Commit above 86%. Stays until it falls below 82%'; CPU 'above 86% ... below 80%'; 'Memory tightening | Warning | Commit above 74%'; 'No bottleneck | Healthy'. brief.html:5388-5392 mock code: "if(S.freq<0.8)v='thermal'; else if(mp>0.86||(v==='mem'&&mp>0.82))v='mem'; else if(cp>0.86||(v==='cpu'&&cp>0.8))v='cpu'". docs/07:97-102: CPU 'CPU time above 85%'; Memory 'Commit above 85% of limit, page writes rising'; Thermal 'Frequency below 80% of maximum under load'; Inconclusive 'Signals disagree' (the lead cites :175-182). docs/17:157 lists six classes and no healthy result; docs/01:13 'reads Inconclusive when the signals disagree'; docs/08:94 'see verdict table'. config.py:143 'thresholds: dict[str, float]'. verify-5/config_and_baseline.out.txt: "verdict.thresholds.cpu_tyme = 0.85 accepted", while 'verdict.thresold (misspelt group) refused'; 'max 4.80 GHz, base 1.80 GHz = 37.5% of max; 80% of max is 3.84 GHz'. docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/pm/intel_pstate.html (re-fetched): 'One important property of turbo P-states is that they are not sustainable.'
findings.impact: Job 2: a builder following docs/07 or docs/17 has no result for a healthy machine. With first-match order, Inconclusive never occurs, and 'disagree' cannot be written as a fixture. If 'maximum' is read as the turbo maximum, a laptop under sustained all-core load reads 'Thermally throttled'; this machine's base frequency is 37.5% of its maximum. A misspelt threshold key silently leaves the default in place, against docs/08:5 'unknown keys are rejected'.
findings.proposed_change: docs/07: make its table the single rule set. Add 'No bottleneck / Healthy' for when no rule matches and there are at least 60 s of data. Define maximum as the base (nominal) frequency, or as the sustained all-core frequency measured in P0, and keep 'under load'. Define 'disagree' as two or more rules matching, or a rule matching while its ruled-out condition holds, and say the verdict is then Inconclusive. Give each threshold its on and off values (hysteresis). docs/02 'How the verdict is chosen': say it is the mock's simplification and point to docs/07. docs/08:94: 'see the verdict table in docs/07'. core/config.py: Verdict.thresholds becomes a model with named fields.
findings.cost: About 15 lines of docs and about 15 lines in config.py.
findings.verification: Re-read docs/02:56-79, docs/07:93-104, docs/17:157, docs/08:5,94 and brief.html:5386-5392. Ran config_and_baseline.py: an unknown threshold key is accepted. Read the sysfs cpufreq files (read-only). Re-fetched the intel_pstate page; the quote is present. Refutation: docs/02:5 and :79 say the mock is synthetic and that its evidence numbers follow the simulation, so docs/02's table describes the mock's code rather than a spec. Even so, docs/02:69 presents it as how the verdict is chosen, and it is the only place with a healthy result. docs/07:104 calls the thresholds starting points, which explains 85 against 86 but not different classes, order and hysteresis. The Windows meaning of 'maximum' was not verified. Severity kept at medium.

findings.title: P0's WSL/Docker rule does not say what the 10% is a share of, or who measures the working day
findings.evidence: docs/15:9 'The share of CPU time held by a WSL2 or Docker VM is reported'; docs/15:45 'Phase 0 reports the VM's share of CPU time over a working day. Above 10%, the guest collector moves to directly after phase 2 ... | Nothing to change. The rule applies itself'; docs/17:264 'report what share of CPU time a WSL2 or Docker Desktop VM holds over a working day. If it is above 10%, tell me'; docs/17:266 'you can only run one OS yourself'. reconcile_terms.out.txt: 'machine busy (per-core counters) 53.96 CPU-s = 22.12% of capacity', so 10% of busy time is about 2.2% of capacity.
findings.impact: The phase-7 decision can flip with the denominator: busy time and capacity differ by about 4.5x on this machine. From CI runners the builder cannot measure the owner's working day, or the per-process VRAM check (docs/15:9), so the P0 gate needs the owner to run a script. No displayed number changes; what changes is when agents running in WSL become attributable (job 1).
findings.proposed_change: docs/15:45 and docs/17:264: 'share of the machine's busy CPU time held by the VM process (vmmem, vmmemWSL), over at least 8 hours of normal use, measured by a script the builder supplies and the owner runs; the per-process VRAM check likewise'. Report the share against both busy time and capacity.
findings.cost: Two sentences in docs/15 and docs/17.
findings.decision_question: Should the 10% be measured against busy CPU time or against total capacity? Recommendation: busy time, because the question is how much of the work happens out of view.
findings.verification: Re-read docs/15:9,45 and docs/17:264,266,268. Searched docs/ for 'working day': only these places. Refutation: docs/17:264 says 'tell me', so the owner sees the figure and decides; 'the rule applies itself' is overstated rather than harmful. Downgraded from medium to low. R10 assigns the 24-hour soak to the owner but not the P0 measurements, so no earlier finding covers this.

findings.title: histogram.percentile(q=100) returns the top of the scale (256 cores) for about a quarter of time-weighted buckets
findings.evidence: core/histogram.py:77 'total = sum(counts)' (sum() of floats is compensated in Python 3.12 and later; pyproject requires >=3.12), :80 'target = total * min(max(q, 0.0), 100.0) / 100.0', :85 'if running + count >= target', :91 'running += count' (plain addition), :92 'return scale.high'. uv run python docs/review/probes/verify-5/rollup_and_histogram.py: 'q=100 returned 256 cores (top of scale) in 276' of 1000 buckets with weights of 0.995 to 1.005 s; 'control, integer weights of exactly 1.0 s: q=100 gives 4.14 cores'; 'fsum vs plain loop on 0.1 x 10: 1.0, (0.9999999999999999, 1.0)'. e-baseline/rollup_cases.py rerun identical: '469 report a maximum of 256 cores'.
findings.impact: Bucket (core/models.py:150-175) has no CPU maximum field, so the CPU minimum-to-maximum envelope that docs/17:132 requires can come only from cores_percentile(q=0 and q=100). About a quarter of buckets would show 256 cores. There is no caller yet. Secondary problem: values below the scale's low edge are read by interpolating within [0, low), so a steady 1 MiB and a steady 15 MiB both read p50 = 8.0 MiB, and 0.002 cores reads 0.005. That contradicts histogram.py:8-9 'within one bin of the true value: a factor of about 1.17'.
findings.proposed_change: core/histogram.py percentile: when the loop ends without a match, or when q >= 100, return the upper edge of the last non-empty bin; add a test with float weights. docs/14 histogram entry: say that a value below the low edge reads as somewhere in [0, low), and that the 1.17 factor holds only inside the scale.
findings.verification: Re-read histogram.py:73-92. Wrote my own probe with float weights of 0.995 to 1.005 s, as a monotonic-clock interval would give: 276 of 1000 buckets return 256 cores, and none do with exact 1.0 weights. That confirms float rounding as the cause: compensated sum() against a plain loop, plus target computed as total*100/100. Grepped src for callers: only cores_percentile and memory_percentile (rollup.py:164,168), which only tests use. Severity kept at medium: the bug is latent with no caller, though the CPU envelope makes a caller likely.

findings.title: Baselines must be kept 'separately for idle and active states', but no document defines idle or active for a workload, and the usual-range window is stated both as 14 values and as 14 days
findings.evidence: docs/17:156 'keep baselines separately for idle and active states'; docs/16:121 (R11 fix); docs/04:30 'Baselines learned separately for idle and active use'; docs/06:39 'Active seconds, so idle and busy periods can be compared separately'. Three unrelated candidates: docs/08:64 idle_after (machine level), docs/08:65 hot_cpu_threshold 0.5% (per process), store/rollup.py:37,68 active_share = 0.005 (per series, tied to no setting). Window: docs/07:36 'the median of the last 14 values that were not flagged'; docs/06:65 '14 d back'; docs/17:156 'over a trailing 14 days'; docs/08:91 baseline.window 14d. A grep of docs/ for idle or active definitions, excluding interval names, finds only these lines; the glossary (docs/12:9) defines only hot and cold sets.
findings.impact: Two builders will split idle and active differently, so no fixture can specify the baseline anomaly detector (job 3), and R11's false-alarm fix depends on that split. On minute buckets, '14 values' and '14 days' differ by a factor of 1440.
findings.proposed_change: docs/07 baseline section: 'a minute bucket is active when active_s is at least half of covered_s, where a sample is active when the workload uses at least hot_cpu_threshold of one core; idle and active baselines use only buckets of their own state'. Tie rollup.py's active_share to sampling.hot_cpu_threshold, and note it in docs/14. State one window rule, for example the last 14 days of unflagged values of the statistic named in M6.
findings.cost: Four sentences in docs/07, one line in rollup.py.
findings.verification: Grepped docs/ for idle and active definitions: only the lines cited. Re-read rollup.py:37,68 and growth.py:87-99. Refutation: the lead's sub-claim that min_values=5 conflicts with the 7-day learning period does not hold, because the detector can enforce learning_period separately and usual_range's min_values is only a floor beneath it; that sub-claim is dropped. The rest stands.

findings.title: The overhead budget covers the collector in docs/08 and 'the monitor' in docs/17, the 150 MB memory budget exists only in docs/17, and the 'submeter' workload holds one pid
findings.evidence: docs/08:140 overhead_fraction 'The collector's CPU time as a share of one core'; docs/08:33 'until the collector is back under 3%'; docs/08:22 'plus 0.2 points for the store and the API' (the API runs in the server, docs/17:53); docs/17:230 'The monitor must not become the problem ... under 1% of one core at idle cadence, under 3% at active cadence, and under 150 MB of memory across collector and server'; docs/15:13 'stays inside the budget' names no budget; docs/11:22's 80 MB is the Rust trigger. attribution/rules.py:124,174 take a single self_pid. verify-5/config_and_baseline.out.txt: 'pid 100: submeter (submeter itself)' / 'pid 200: unattributed (no rule matched)' for a submeter-server process. docs/04:17 'Submeter itself always shown'. No shipped rule claims the server (docs/08:219-252).
findings.impact: The P1 soak gate cannot be judged without knowing which processes and which memory figure count. The server's rollups, analysis and API land in Unattributed, so Submeter under-reports its own cost, and the built-in 'submeter over budget' alert (docs/08:150) ignores the server.
findings.proposed_change: docs/08 after overhead_limit, docs/08:140 and docs/15:13: state that the budget covers every Submeter process (collector, server and launcher holders). Their summed CPU stays under 1% of one core at idle cadence and 3% at active cadence, and memory stays under 150 MB across collector and server, with the figure named (private bytes on Windows, USS on Linux). The overhead guard acts on the collector; overhead_fraction reports the total. docs/14 attribution entry and rules.py: the submeter workload claims every Submeter process (a set of pids or an executable match), not one pid.
findings.cost: About three sentences in docs/08 and docs/15, one in docs/14; a few lines in rules.py.
findings.decision_question: Does the overhead budget cover only the collector, or every Submeter process (collector plus server plus launcher holders)? Recommendation: every Submeter process, because docs/17:230 says 'the monitor' and the server's work is real overhead on the machine.
findings.verification: Re-read docs/08:22,33,72,140,150, docs/17:53,230, docs/15:13 and rules.py:118-128,168-176. Ran the Attributor with self_pid on two Submeter processes: the server process is unattributed. Searched docs/ for a memory budget: only docs/17:230; docs/11:22's 80 MB is a switching rule. Refutation: 'across collector and server' in docs/17:230 can be read as qualifying memory only, and that ambiguity is the finding itself. A user rule in rules.toml could claim the server, but no shipped rule does.
